of perspiration as it was a gift from God. â€œBetter landâ€, therefore, was

text: Nonetheless, attempts to control for the quality of land can be carried out.
text_raw:
Nonetheless, attempts to control for the quality of land can be carried 
out.

text: A number of different proxies for land quality were used and tested in two specifications: land quality was entered as a separate independent variable and a standardized land quality variable was used to transform the land/labor ratio into â€œefficiency unitsâ€.
text_raw:
A number of different proxies for land quality were used and tested 
in two specifications: land quality was entered as a separate independent 
variable and a standardized land quality variable was used to transform 
the land/labor ratio into â€œefficiency unitsâ€.

text: The proxies for land quality experimented with were:
text_raw:
The proxies for land quality 
experimented with were:

text: (1) The proportion of land under cultivation.
text_raw: (1) The proportion of land under cultivation.

text: The use of this proxy assumes that the quality of land within each county is distributed uniformly over the surface, and that the threshold level at which land is brought into cultivation is a function of the other indepenÂ¬ dent variables in the regression.
text_raw:
The use of this proxy 
assumes that the quality of land within each county is distributed 
uniformly over the surface, and that the threshold level at which 
land is brought into cultivation is a function of the other indepenÂ¬ 
dent variables in the regression.

text: The proportion under cultivation is a function of the mean quality of the land and the threshold level.
text_raw:
The proportion under cultivation 
is a function of the mean quality of the land and the threshold level.

text: If we solve for the latter, the proportion of land under cultivation can be interpreted as a function of the average quality of the land.
text_raw:
If we solve for the latter, the proportion of land under cultivation 
can be interpreted as a function of the average quality of the land.

text: (2) A transformation of the proportion land under cultivation derived from the normal distribution.
text_raw:
(2) A transformation of the proportion land under cultivation derived 
from the normal distribution.

text: This variable is similar to the previous one except that the distribution of land quality is assumed normal.
text_raw:
This variable is similar to the 
previous one except that the distribution of land quality is assumed 
normal.

text: The precise assumptions underlying proxies 1 and 2 and the derivation of the estimated equations are presented in Appendix B to this chapter.
text_raw:
The precise assumptions underlying proxies 1 and 2 and 
the derivation of the estimated equations are presented in 
Appendix B to this chapter.

text: (3) The mean elevation above sea-level, capturing the lower fertility of mountainous areas and highlands (Andrews, 1980, p.
text_raw:
(3) The mean elevation above sea-level, capturing the lower fertility of 
mountainous areas and highlands (Andrews, 1980, p.

text: (4) The variance of the elevation above sea-level.
text_raw: (4) The variance of the elevation above sea-level.

text: This variable captures altitude as well, but in addition captures the variability and unevenness of the terrain.
text_raw:
This variable 
captures altitude as well, but in addition captures the variability 
and unevenness of the terrain.

text: (5) Rents per acre.
text_raw: (5) Rents per acre.

text: This assumes a purely Ricardian model of rents, in which labor and other factors are assumed to be perfectly mobile and differences in rent reflect differences in land quality only.
text_raw:
This assumes a purely Ricardian model of rents, in 
which labor and other factors are assumed to be perfectly mobile 
and differences in rent reflect differences in land quality only.

text: (6) The proportion uncultivated land which is â€œunimprovable for cultivationâ€.
text_raw:
(6) The proportion uncultivated land which is â€œunimprovable for 
cultivationâ€.

text: The higher this proportion, the lower the quality of land not under cultivation, which should reflectâ€”other things equalâ€”the quality of the land presently under cultivation.
text_raw:
The higher this proportion, the lower the quality of 
land not under cultivation, which should reflectâ€”other things 
equalâ€”the quality of the land presently under cultivation.

text_raw:

versions of this measure were used, namely, the proportion

text: 48 WHY IRELAND STARVED unimprovable land relative to the size of the county, and the proportion relative to total â€œUnimproved pasture and bog landsâ€, as defined by the General Valuation Office in Dublin.

text: The results of the attempts to examine the Malthusian hypothesis while controlling for land quality are presented in Tables 3.8 and 3.9.
text_raw:
The results of the attempts to examine the Malthusian hypothesis 
while controlling for land quality are presented in Tables 3.8 and 3.9.

text: In Table 3.8 the various measures of land quality are allowed to enter the regression equation unconstrained.
text_raw:
In 
Table 3.8 the various measures of land quality are allowed to enter the 
regression equation unconstrained.

text: In columns 1 and 2 the variables are purely physical.
text_raw:
In columns 1 and 2 the variables are 
purely physical.

text: One of them has an insignificant coefficient, the other one has the wrong sign.
text_raw:
One of them has an insignificant coefficient, the other 
one has the wrong sign.

text: In columns 3 and 4 the proportion under cultivation (or 0, which is a function of it) are used, without much more success.
text_raw:
In columns 3 and 4 the proportion under 
cultivation (or 0, which is a function of it) are used, without much more 
success.

text: This is probably due to the assumption imposed on columns 3 and 4 that the standard deviation of the quality index is constant.
text_raw:
This is probably due to the assumption imposed on columns 3 
and 4 that the standard deviation of the quality index is constant.

text: Relaxing that assumption results in columns 5 and 6, in which the land- quality index is significant at the 1 percent level and has the expected sign.
text_raw:
Relaxing that assumption results in columns 5 and 6, in which the land- 
quality index is significant at the 1 percent level and has the expected 
sign.

text: The other three measures of land quality, rents per acre and two variants of the proportion of unimprovable land all have the expected signs, but are not very strong statistically.
text_raw:
The other three measures of land quality, rents per acre and two 
variants of the proportion of unimprovable land all have the expected 
signs, but are not very strong statistically.

text: In none of the nine columns does the inclusion of quality variables have the slightest effect on the seemingly perverse behavior of the population pressure variable (PPV), defined here as the land-labor ratio, or the number of acres under cultivation divided by the rural population.
text_raw:
In none of the nine columns 
does the inclusion of quality variables have the slightest effect on the 
seemingly perverse behavior of the population pressure variable (PPV), 
defined here as the land-labor ratio, or the number of acres under 
cultivation divided by the rural population.

text: In Table 3.9 the quantity and quality of land are entered jointly by defining land â€œin efficiency unitsâ€, which is accomplished by multiplying the land-labor ratio by indices of land quality if these indices measure quality directly, or dividing the land-labor ratio by the quality indices if they measure quality inversely.
text_raw:
In Table 3.9 the quantity 
and quality of land are entered jointly by defining land â€œin efficiency 
unitsâ€, which is accomplished by multiplying the land-labor ratio by 
indices of land quality if these indices measure quality directly, or 
dividing the land-labor ratio by the quality indices if they measure 
quality inversely.

text: The result is that the perversely significant wrong sign on the land-labor ratio disappears in most cases, and its coefficients sink into statistical insignificance.
text_raw:
The result is that the perversely significant wrong sign 
on the land-labor ratio disappears in most cases, and its coefficients sink 
into statistical insignificance.

text: The conclusion suggested by these data is therefore that land appears to have been less of a binding constraint on the Irish economy than the â€œoverpopulationâ€ view would have us believe.
text_raw:
The conclusion suggested by these data is therefore that land appears 
to have been less of a binding constraint on the Irish economy than the 
â€œoverpopulationâ€ view would have us believe.

text: In view of the assumpÂ¬ tions we have had to make to carry out the tests described in Tables 3.7-3.9, this conclusion should be regarded with some caution.
text_raw:
In view of the assumpÂ¬ 
tions we have had to make to carry out the tests described in Tables 
3.7-3.9, this conclusion should be regarded with some caution.

text: There appears to be no statistically significant relation between poverty (as measured by our estimated personal income series) and population pressure variables.
text_raw:
There 
appears to be no statistically significant relation between poverty (as 
measured by our estimated personal income series) and population 
pressure variables.

text: The procedure followed was to assume that the land-labor ratio was exogenous and income endogenous, which proÂ¬ duced a testable implication.
text_raw:
The procedure followed was to assume that the 
land-labor ratio was exogenous and income endogenous, which proÂ¬ 
duced a testable implication.

text: The implication was tested and found inconsistent with the evidence.
text_raw:
The implication was tested and found 
inconsistent with the evidence.

text: This, of course, is not the same as arguing thafâ€œland did not matterâ€ which would be a rash inference from our data.
text_raw:
This, of course, is not the same as 
arguing thafâ€œland did not matterâ€ which would be a rash inference from 
our data.

text: Nor does it follow that a reduction of population size may not have meant more income per capita if such a reduction had somehow been carried out in a costless and frictionless way.
text_raw:
Nor does it follow that a reduction of population size may not 
have meant more income per capita if such a reduction had somehow 
been carried out in a costless and frictionless way.

text: The economy contains, after all, three factors of production.
text_raw:
The economy 
contains, after all, three factors of production.

text: Reducing labor increases the capital-labor ratio and through that mechanism leads to higher incomes.
text_raw:
Reducing labor increases 
the capital-labor ratio and through that mechanism leads to higher 
incomes.

text: A few negative results are rather striking: religion seems to have no influence whatsoever on the propensity to marry.

seems to have no influence whatsoever on the propensity to marry.

text: Holding other factors equal, the proportion Catholics in each county, which varied from 98T4 percent in Clare to 28*24 percent in Antrim, has no discernible effect on the various measures.

text: Nor do the occupaÂ¬ tional structure (as measured by the proportion families employed predominantly in manufacturing) or the agricultural capital-labor ratio (as measured by the value of livestock per rural inhabitant).

text: Cottage industry, often claimed to be a central factor in the marriage behavior of society, does not appear very significant, but still seems to have the expected effect as far as males are concerned.
text_raw:

behavior of society, does not appear very significant, but still seems to 
have the expected effect as far as males are concerned.

text: The female propensity to marry appears unaffected by it.

propensity to marry appears unaffected by it.

text: Insofar as birth rates were far more affected by the female propensity to marry, this result underÂ¬ mines the view that cottage industry greatly stimulated population growth by reducing the average age at marriage.

far more affected by the female propensity to marry, this result underÂ¬

text: For income, the reverse is true: the male propensity to marry seems independent of the level of income per capita, while the â€œConnell-effectâ€, which links early marriage to poverty, seems to be operative for women.

text: Even more surprising is the result that the dependency on potatoes does not seem to have a significant effect on the male propensity to marry, but apparently led to later and fewer marriages among women.
text_raw:

surprising is the result that the dependency on potatoes does not seem to 
have a significant effect on the male propensity to marry, but apparently 
led to later and fewer marriages among women.

text: This, indeed, is a perplexing result, until one recalls the increasing difficulty of securing potato land on the eve of the famine.

perplexing result, until one recalls the increasing difficulty of securing 
potato land on the eve of the famine.

text: High potato acreage could mean that most of the land which was appropriate for small-scale tillage farms was already in use and that landlords were reluctant to provide more.

text: It is not clear, however, why that would affect women but not men.

text: The proximity of urban areas, with the perceived opportunities they provided to males, leads to significantly increased propensities to marry.
text_raw:

provided to males, leads to significantly increased propensities to marry.

text: The quality of housing variable strongly affects the propensity to marry: a large supply of cheap, fourth-class houses reduced the price of forming a family and thus enabled the average Irishman or Irishwoman to marry younger.

a large supply of cheap, fourth-class houses reduced the price of forming
